Neonatal specimens of the Western wobbegong, Orectolobus hutchinsi, emerge from their egg cases at a total length ranging from 22 to 26 cm (22-26 cm) [Lb = 22-26 cm], which represents a modest size at birth compared to certain other orectolobid species. These young sharks, during the initial stages of their life history, rely entirely upon endogenous yolk reserves until the process of yolk-sac resorption is complete and the transition to active feeding on small benthic invertebrates begins. The weight at birth for these pups has been documented at 78.7 grams [Wwb = 78.7 grams], a value that reflects the considerable energy invested by the gravid female into each individual offspring. Within the controlled environment of a laboratory aquarium maintained at a stable water temperature of 18.3 °C [T = 18.3 °C], the embryonic development period from egg deposition to the point of hatching was observed to be 353 days [ab = 353 days], an exceptionally protracted gestation-like phase that is characteristic of many slow-growing, late-maturing elasmobranchs. This extended incubation period is thought to contribute to the relatively advanced state of the free-swimming pup.

As the juveniles progress through their sub-adult phase, they undergo a dramatic increase in body mass, with the ultimate wet weight for this species being calculated at approximately 23.5 kilograms [Wwi = approximately 23.5 kilograms]. This asymptotic mass, derived from a length–weight relationship, underscores the robustly built, dorso-ventrally flattened body plan that these ambush predators possess. The onset of puberty, which marks the transition to a reproductively active adult capable of insemination, is reached when males attain a total length of 112 cm [Lp = 112 cm]. This length threshold is slightly higher than the general total length at puberty of 110 cm [Lp = 110 cm] observed across both sexes when combined, indicating a subtle degree of sexual dimorphism in the timing of gonadal maturation. The attainment of these sizes is a gradual process, reflecting the species' energetically conservative lifestyle, where they spend considerable time motionless on the seafloor, relying on cryptic coloration to ambush prey.

Within the stable thermal conditions of 18.3 °C [T = 18.3 °C] that define their temperate reef habitat, the overall life history is paced at an extremely slow tempo. The maximum recorded longevity for this species, derived from captive observations under these conditions, reaches an impressive 25 years [am = 25 years], a lifespan that is quite substantial for a shark of its moderate dimensions at a temperature of 18.3 °C [T = 18.3 °C]. This extended period of survival is coupled with a remarkably low annual reproductive output, which is characteristic of many benthic elasmobranchs that invest heavily in a small number of high-quality offspring. The maximum reproductive rate, recorded at this stable temperature, is best expressed through the interaction of fecundity and frequency. Females typically produce a single litter of approximately 25 pups per reproductive event [N_R_i = approximately 25 pups per reproductive event], with a frequency of one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year], which corresponds to a daily reproductive rate of approximately 0.068 pups per day [Ri = approximately 0.068 pups per day], leading to a very low intrinsic rate of population increase.

A comprehensive understanding of the species' growth trajectory requires examination of its ultimate total length, which has been recorded at 149 cm [Li = 149 cm] for mature adults. This value represents the maximum total length that an individual of Orectolobus hutchinsi can be expected to attain, marking the endpoint of its somatic growth curve. The relatively slow growth rate required to reach this size is consistent with the extended developmental timeline already noted. The time needed to progress from the neonate stage, through the juvenile and sub-adult phases, to the point of first reproduction is a critical aspect of the species' demography. Given the extended gestation period of 353 days and the delayed attainment of the size necessary for sexual maturity, it is evident that the generation time is quite long. This slow pace of life makes the Western wobbegong particularly vulnerable to population declines from overfishing, as the capacity for rapid population recovery is extremely limited.

The demography of Orectolobus hutchinsi is profoundly influenced by its life-history strategy, which prioritizes longevity and offspring quality over high fecundity. The contrast between the modest size at birth, ranging from 22 to 26 cm (22-26 cm) [Lb = 22-26 cm], and the ultimate adult size of 149 cm [Li = 149 cm] reveals a substantial scope for growth over the species' extended lifespan. Field surveys indicate that males begin their reproductive careers upon crossing the size threshold of 112 cm [Lp = 112 cm] in total length, while the general population data suggests a slightly lower estimate of 110 cm [Lp = 110 cm] when including females. The considerable energetic investment per offspring, evidenced by the birth weight of 78.7 grams [Wwb = 78.7 grams] and the adult asymptotic mass of 23.5 kilograms [Wwi = 23.5 kilograms], places this species firmly at the slow end of the elasmobranch life-history continuum, making habitat conservation and careful fisheries management essential for its long-term persistence.
